title: Orders close: many rooms
hookLine: five families of prayer, one house: looking back on the great orders

lines: A BELL, A FRIAR, A BOOK.
cards: A bell in a monastery calling monks from the garden to the chapel. A barefoot friar, patient and glad in the cold. A preacher with a book under his arm.
A soldier-turned-pilgrim asking what stirs in his heart. A hermit's cell on a mountain, and a silence you could lean against.
That's the road this block has walked: the great orders of the Catholic Church, one family after another. Now, at the end of the corridor, a look back at all the doors. Today, the orders close.

teach.b: First, Benedict's balance. Ora et labora, pray and work: a day where the bell, the psalm, the garden and the meal each get their place, and none swallows the rest. Second, Francis's joy.
Not a cheerful mood, but perfect joy, the kind that stays patient even when you're turned away in the cold.
Third, Dominic's truth. Veritas, the order's motto: pray, study, and then share what you've found, because truth is meant to be handed on.
Fourth, Ignatius's discernment, reading the movements of the heart to find God in all things.
And fifth, Carmel's silence: the cell, the desert, the friend, the night, and simple loving attention. Five families, five ways in. Now the image that holds them.

teach.h: IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE, MANY MANSIONS.
teach.b: At the Last Supper, Jesus tells his friends, in the Douay-Rheims: "In my Father's house there are many mansions." Many rooms, one house.
The Church doesn't ask anyone to live in all five rooms at once, and it doesn't rank them. Saint Paul tells the Corinthians: "Now there are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit."
A Benedictine and a Jesuit pray very differently, and both are at home. That's the surprise of this block: the orders aren't rival teams.
They're rooms in one house, and a person can be drawn to one room for a season of life, then find another door opening years later. Not everyone will take vows.
But anyone can borrow a room: an hour of balance, a moment of joy, one shared truth, a nightly examen, a few minutes of silence.

how: Catholics who aren't in religious life often draw on one order's spirituality: some become oblates of a Benedictine monastery, secular Franciscans, lay Dominicans or Secular Carmelites, or keep an Ignatian examen, while staying in their parish.

games.why: many rooms, one house. the orders aren't rival teams; a person can live in one room for a season, and another door may open later.

practice: Walk slowly past each door in your mind: Benedict's balance of work and prayer, Francis's joy and simplicity, Dominic's study and one shared truth, Ignatius's nightly examen, Carmel's few minutes of silent, loving attention.

Don't pick the one that sounds most impressive; notice which door your heart leans toward this month, and stop there. If you pray, ask God to show you the room for this season; if you don't, simply trust the lean.

wordCard.voice: Orders close. The end of the great orders: Benedict's balance, Francis's joy, Dominic's truth, Ignatius's discernment, Carmel's silence, rooms in one house. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: dwelling places, rooms, the word behind mansions in John 14:2.
